title: {{NAME}} and the Paw Patrol of Parkside
moral: You don't need a cape to be someone's hero, just show up when they need you.

pages.content:
{{NAME}}'s superpower was being extremely good at noticing things other people missed.

He noticed: the stray cat under the library steps who only came out for cheese-flavoured crackers. The injured pigeon in the park who held one wing slightly wrong. The old dog on Maple Street whose water bowl was always dry by noon.

He fixed what he could fix. He got a reputation.

That was how the animal shelter gave him his own key at age nine and called him: Guardian of Parkside.

pages.content:
The emergency came on a Thursday.

A storm had flooded the lower part of Greystone Park where the small-animal dens were, and six different families needed relocating before the second rain band came in at midnight.

The shelter was full. The vet was an hour away.

{{NAME}} pulled on his cape, packed his bag, and ran.

What he found was a chaos of frightened rabbits, confused hedgehogs, and one extremely wet family of ducks who had technically been fine but objected to the principle of the whole situation.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} worked until ten o'clock.

He built a temporary nest from a waterproof bag and dry leaves for the rabbit family. He carried the hedgehogs one by one to the park shelter shed. He negotiated with the ducks for twenty minutes before accepting that they were absolutely fine and had only staged a crisis for attention.

"You're fine," he told them sternly. They quacked.

He built the last nest by torchlight, knees wet, cape dripping, completely satisfied.

pages.content:
By eleven, every animal was settled.

The rabbits were snug. The hedgehogs were dry. The ducks had waddled back to their preferred spot and arranged themselves with dignity.

{{NAME}} sat in the shed doorway and watched the rain start again, heavy and grey over the park.

The rabbit mother came to the door of her nest and looked at him.

{{NAME}} nodded. "You're safe," he said.

She went back inside.

He sat a while longer, listening to rain on the roof, feeling quietly enormous.

pages.content:
He got home at eleven thirty, soaking wet, and his mum wrapped him in a towel and made him cocoa without asking any questions, which was the best parenting he had ever witnessed.

In his room, cape on the chair, he lay in the warm dark.

Outside, the rain drummed on. Inside, safe.

He thought about the rabbit mother looking at him from the nest door. That one look.

He closed his eyes, and just before sleep, he thought he heard something: very small, very faint, from somewhere out in the dark and the rain, a sound that might have been rabbits, warm and dry, safe.
